Methionine is required to enter the cycle. This does not show that raising methionine intake increases human remethylation or transsulfuration rates.

A formula that removed methionine and cysteine together slowed whole-blood synthesis, so that result does not isolate methionine. In the cysteine-free study, methionine intake stayed adequate and red-cell synthesis did not fall. This does not show that eating more methionine, once intake is adequate, raises glutathione synthesis.

Endogenous remethylation also supplies methionine. Neonatal-piglet isotope incorporation does not establish an adult intake target, cerebral delivery or benefit above adequacy. Methyl allocation, SAH inhibition, transport and other substrate availability constrain the route; no shared KC admission follows.

Human MAT structural and enzymological evidence establishes catalytic capacity. Ordinary food supply is distinct from measured MAT flux; no benefit from additional magnesium in replete people or universal methylation increase is asserted.

Human GSS crystallography and cofactor annotation support capacity. The structure contains two magnesium ions; this does not establish a dietary dose, increased blood or neuronal glutathione synthesis, or benefit above adequacy. Original one-per-subunit wording is retained in history rather than used as dietary stoichiometry.

Human MAT structures establish the specific ion relationship. Physiological potassium homeostasis and tissue uptake intervene; no claim that extra dietary potassium raises SAM flux or improves methylation is established.

In nine healthy young adults, 28 days of vitamin B6 restriction lowered plasma pyridoxal phosphate and did not change mean postprandial remethylation, transmethylation, or total transsulfuration rates.

Salvage of food vitamin B6 to pyridoxal 5'-phosphate does not show that higher vitamin B6 intake increases cystathionine beta-synthase or cystathionine gamma-lyase flux. Moderate B6 restriction changed cystathionine handling but did not significantly reduce total transsulfuration in the assessed human tracer study.

Endogenous glycine synthesis and other methyltransferases also contribute. Enzyme loss is not glycine deficiency; extra dietary glycine has not been established to normalise whole-cycle or brain methylation.
In older adults glycine was supplemented together with a cysteine precursor, so that rise in erythrocyte synthesis does not isolate glycine.

Purified-enzyme dependence on pyridoxal 5'-phosphate does not show that raising vitamin B6 intake increases cysteine formation in people. Moderate B6 restriction changed cystathionine handling but did not significantly reduce total transsulfuration in the assessed human tracer study.
Serine is a direct enzyme substrate. Endogenous synthesis and diet can both supply it; this does not show that dietary serine or protein intake increases cystathionine formation.

Cysteine is the substrate of the first assembly step. A formula that removed methionine and cysteine together slowed whole-blood synthesis, and that formula also removed methionine. When methionine intake stayed adequate, removing cysteine did not lower red-cell synthesis in young men. This does not show that eating more cysteine, once intake is adequate, raises glutathione synthesis.
No human study in this assessment showed that changing dietary glutamate changes glutathione synthesis.

The synthesis increase was measured in older adults given this precursor together with glycine. It does not show an effect of N-acetylcysteine alone, of ordinary foods, or of supplementation outside that group, and it is not a neuronal or clinical result.
Plasma tracing does not measure absolute hepatic flux, intermediary SAM, ordinary-food equivalence or benefit.

Uridine is a supported precursor source, not an indispensable dietary requirement: endogenous nucleotide synthesis and salvage also supply CTP. Rat-slice and oral-UMP gerbil results do not establish an ordinary-food dose, increased human PC flux or cognitive benefit; human MRS measures precursor pools.

Reviewed UniProt IKBKB records the ATP-dependent IκB kinase reaction without a magnesium cofactor annotation; published IKKβ crystals used in this review are inhibitor-bound rather than ATP–Mg ternary complexes. This does not establish that ordinary dietary magnesium intake limits human NF-κB transcription.

Cellular redox studies show context-dependent effects, including inhibition after glutathione depletion or increased extracellular cysteine. Neither individual dietary limitation, brain transfer nor benefit from additional intake is established.

In Salmonella-infected rats, glutathione depletion did not increase permeability or bacterial translocation. Neither intestinal precursor inadequacy, individual constituent limitation, human LPS reduction nor benefit from additional intake is established.

Human target engagement varies by formulation, tissue and population. The positive study used a myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate for three days in healthy nonsmokers and measured nasal phase II enzyme RNA, not Nrf2 protein or nuclear translocation. Extract capsules did not increase lung target-gene expression in COPD. An ordinary broccoli meal, direct activation of Nrf2 in the human brain and clinical ADHD benefit remain unestablished. Sulforaphane is not an essential nutrient.

In selenium-deficient adults, plasma glutathione peroxidase activity levelled off once intake reached about 35 micrograms a day. Intake above that plateau did not raise the enzyme further, and the study did not measure net oxidative pressure.

Mouse whole-organ enzyme assays do not identify mitochondrial isoforms, a human food dose or benefit above selenium adequacy. Repletion response depended on dose; antioxidant capacity does not establish clinical prevention.
Culture selenium exposure is not an oral food dose. This supports the thioredoxin arm, not selenium dependence of glutathione reductase, universal tissue recycling flux or benefit above adequacy.

Curated human SOD1 and experimental structural evidence support a structural capacity relationship, not zinc-dependent catalysis identical to copper. Erythrocyte superoxide dismutase rose after copper repletion in infants with marginal copper status. That does not show that extra copper raises the enzyme when status is already adequate.

Human SOD2 requires manganese; dietary depletion experiments measured lower heart and kidney MnSOD activity in rats. This establishes a bounded enzyme-capacity dependency, not a human dose recommendation, universal tissue response, measured net ROS balance or benefit above adequate intake.

Rat diet and tissue context; the kidney result is not a uniform response across organs or a human intake threshold. Human catalase haem identity supports capacity, not benefit from extra iron. Iron can also promote non-enzymatic oxidation; higher catalase activity is not a clinical benefit.

Vitamin E breaks peroxyl-radical chains in membranes. That chemistry does not show that extra vitamin E lowers peroxidation in people. A prevention trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU a day.
Regeneration of the vitamin E radical is not a high-dose rule. A prevention trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU of vitamin E a day.

pm_inventory.mission: Synchronise the central circadian clock with the external light–dark cycle through retinal light signals.
Coordinate peripheral metabolic clock timing through feeding cues.
Enable NAPE-to-NAE biosynthesis so endocannabinoidome signalling lipids remain available for stress and motivation regulation.
Sustain omega-3-derived ethanolamide production so endocannabinoidome neuromodulation stays supplied from dietary fat status.
Preserve endocannabinoid signalling duration by limiting FAAH-mediated degradation of anandamide and related NAEs.
Shape dopaminergic reward and motivation pathways through endocannabinoid neuromodulatory interaction.
Sustain endocannabinoid-mediated stress buffering so HPA-axis and neuroinflammatory reactivity stay proportionate.
Maintain stable oestrogen-linked signalling so dopamine tone and emotional regulation remain steady across hormonal fluctuation.
Shape systemic oestrogen exposure through microbiome-mediated regulation of oestrogen metabolism and recycling.
Sustain microbial contributions to progesterone-related hormonal stability through gut ecosystem function.
Enable coordinated integration of insulin and metabolic signalling with reproductive hormone balance.
Maintain androgen receptor signalling so motivation, stamina, and goal-directed effort remain well supported.
Shape systemic androgen exposure through microbiome-mediated androgen metabolism and recycling.
Ensure meal-level protein supply delivers the amino-acid foundation neurotransmitter pathways depend on.
Regulate competitive transport of large neutral amino acids across the blood–brain barrier in response to circulating substrate availability.
Maintain appropriately regulated dopamine synthesis, storage, release, receptor signalling, reuptake and metabolism across changing functional demand.
Support noradrenergic alertness and executive control so attention and arousal stay appropriately engaged.
Support serotonergic signalling so mood stability, inhibition, and behavioural regulation remain well grounded.
Maintain the capacity to form acetylcholine so cholinergic signalling for attention, working memory, and learning stays supplied.
Deliver and integrate DHA into neuronal membranes so the brain maintains a flexible, signal-ready lipid foundation.
Clear and recycle glutamate efficiently so excitatory load does not overwhelm neural circuits.
Limit excitotoxic pressure when glutamatergic drive is excessive so neural stability is protected over time.
Maintain sufficient glutamate decarboxylase capacity, and sufficient PLP cofactor to support it, so GABA can be synthesised from glutamate.
Maintain and adapt physical connections between neurons through synapse formation, selective stabilisation, structural remodelling and elimination.
Recycle homocysteine to methionine through folate and B12 so methyl-donor supply and homocysteine control stay supported.
Provide a parallel homocysteine clearance route so methionine and SAMe supply remain resilient when folate demand is high.
Maintain methionine adenosyltransferase capacity to convert methionine and ATP into SAMe, sustaining the methyl-donor pool used by downstream methyltransferases.
Maintain balanced methionine-cycle flux so methionine availability, SAM-dependent methylation, homocysteine recycling and transsulfuration remain coordinated across changing physiological demand.
Divert homocysteine toward cysteine so methylation demand is balanced against sulfur amino-acid and redox needs.
Build glutathione from sulfur amino acids so cellular antioxidant defence stays connected to one-carbon metabolism.
Maintain phosphatidylcholine formation through PEMT methylation and the choline-based Kennedy pathway.
Regulate NF-κB transcriptional tone so pro-inflammatory gene programmes do not fire excessively.
Limit gut-derived endotoxin spillover so barrier dysfunction does not drive systemic inflammatory load.
Regulate the expression of cellular defence genes in response to oxidative and electrophilic stress.
Balance reactive oxygen species production and clearance so net oxidative pressure stays within tolerable limits.
Protect membrane fats from oxidative damage so vulnerable polyunsaturated fatty acids remain intact.

transformations.process: Digestive lipolysis releases C8 fatty acid from trioctanoin; the absorbed fatty acid is represented as octanoate at physiological pH.
transformations.limitations: The C8 acyl form is not free octanoate content in food. Mixed-chain MCT products have formulation-dependent composition.

evidence.statement: Human triglyceride-lipase reaction provenance and the defined oral tricaprylin exposure; retrieved 26 October 2026.

transformations.process: Hepatic fatty-acid activation and successive mitochondrial beta-oxidation reactions generate acetyl-CoA from the C8 chain.
transformations.limitations: This is a multireaction biological process, not a single chemical reaction. Tissue partitioning and energy state prevent a fixed food-to-acetyl-CoA yield. Cofactor participation creates no separate dietary admissions.

evidence.statement: Human medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase establishes the initial beta-oxidation reaction; the clinical exposure additionally measures downstream ketone provision.

transformations.process: Hepatic mitochondrial ketogenesis proceeds through acetoacetyl-CoA formation, HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA lyase to produce acetoacetate.
dependencies: Ketone release, circulation and brain monocarboxylate transport
transformations.limitations: The endogenous product can interconvert with beta-hydroxybutyrate, but the target identity here is acetoacetate. Ketogenesis, cerebral uptake and ATP production are distinct; no fixed yield or universal benefit is inferred.

evidence.statement: Curated human ACAT1, HMGCS2 and HMGCL reactions, retrieved 26 October 2026.

nutrition_supplementary_sources.label: Sulforaphane
nutrition_supplementary_sources.public_note: One UK broccoli lot, cooked sous vide at 100 °C for 20 minutes, formed 1.06 µmol sulforaphane per g dry weight. Adding 1 g brown mustard powder raised that to 8.58 µmol/g dry weight. Twelve adults who ate 200 g excreted 9.8 µmol sulforaphane-NAC per g creatinine in 24 hours, and 44.7 µmol/g creatinine with the mustard. These figures are not a sulforaphane amount for every 100 g of broccoli.
nutrition_supplementary_sources.source_note: Okunade et al. (2018), Molecular Nutrition & Food Research 62:1700980, Table 1 and the 24-hour urine result. Table 1, µmol sulforaphane per g dry weight: raw 2.05 ± 0.25; sous vide 100 °C for 20 minutes 1.06 ± 0.18; the same cooked broccoli plus 1 g brown mustard powder 8.58 ± 0.33. 8.58 / 1.06 = 8.1, which the paper reports as an 8-fold increase. One results sentence prints the mustard result as 8.58 ± 0.13; the table figure is used here. Urine, 12 adults, 200 g of that cooked broccoli: 9.8 ± 5.1 µmol sulforaphane-NAC per g creatinine in 24 hours without mustard, and 44.7 ± 33.9 with 1 g mustard. 44.7 / 9.8 = 4.6 from the published means. The paper's average of each person's increase is 4.7-fold, with individual increases from 1.7-fold to 10-fold. Sous-vide myrosinase loss in the same paper: 40% after 2 minutes, 90% after 6 minutes, and no measurable activity after 8 minutes. The study did not report a glucoraphanin concentration, and the dry-weight results are not converted to a fresh 100 g amount. Fahey et al. (1997) identifies sulforaphane as the myrosinase product of glucoraphanin; it is not the source of these figures.

calculation.not_a_panel_amount: Dry-weight and creatinine-normalised study results. No moisture figure is given, so they are not scaled to per 100 g fresh broccoli.

nutrition_source.food_name: MCT Premium C8 & C10 100% Pure Oil; declared ingredient "MCT oil (60% C8, 40% C10)"
nutrition_source.selection_reason: MCT oil is a formulated product defined by its specification rather than by an agricultural commodity, so a manufacturer declaration for a single-ingredient product outranks any general composition database — and no general database holds it. The values are chemically constrained by what the product is: a pure triglyceride oil is entirely fat, and both C8:0 and C10:0 are fully saturated, so a saturated fat approaching the total fat is expected rather than surprising. The Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code defines medium chain triglycerides as "triacylglycerols that contain predominantly the saturated fatty acids designated by 8:0 and 10:0", which corroborates the fatty acid class independently of any one brand.
nutrition_source.limitations: Label-derived values from one product, subject to US rounding rules. Energy of 833 kcal per 100 g reflects the lower yield of medium-chain fatty acids, about 8.3 kcal/g, rather than the 9 kcal/g of long-chain fat; a second product (FDC 2426574) declares 867 kcal, so treat the figure as approximate. The C8:C10 ratio is specific to this formulation and varies between brands. Records with a millilitre serving size can be converted to a per-100 g basis on an assumed density of 1.0, which overstates an oil by around 7 per cent; the values here are the internally consistent set for a pure oil by mass. Individual C6, C8 and C10 quantities are not declared.
nutrition_source.previously_withdrawn: USDA FDC 748278, 'Oil, canola', withdrawn 2026-08-18. Canola is a long-chain seed oil, and its saturated fat of 6.61 g and ALA of 7450 mg had been published here. Nothing from that record survives.

nutrition_supplementary_sources.label: MCT
nutrition_supplementary_sources.source_note: MCT oil is defined by its medium-chain triglyceride content, so presence follows from the product identity, and the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code defines the class as triacylglycerols containing predominantly the saturated fatty acids 8:0 and 10:0. The adopted specification (FDC 2543941) declares 60 per cent C8 and 40 per cent C10, but that ratio is particular to one formulation and C6 is not quantified at all, so no per-chain quantity is published for MCT oil in general.
nutrition_supplementary_sources.public_note: MCT oil consists of medium-chain triglycerides; C8/C10 proportions vary with the formulation.

nutrition_supplementary_sources.source_reference: Wang, Riedl and Schwartz (2010), Journal of Chromatography B 878(29), 2949–2958, Table 5
nutrition_supplementary_sources.source_note: Calculated from the reported Table 5 molar sum, not directly reported mass concentration. Includes polyglutamate species as monoglutamate equivalents, not their intact molecular masses. One study sample does not establish universal food composition; do not add this vitamer value to total folate as an independent nutrient supply.

occurrences.evidence: Okunade, Niranjan, Ghawi, Kuhnle and Methven (2018), Molecular Nutrition & Food Research 62:1700980. Formation identity also rests on Fahey et al. (1997).
occurrences.limitations: Sulforaphane forms from glucoraphanin when myrosinase is active. In one cooked-broccoli study the amount depended on preparation, and it is not entered as a per-100 g nutrient.

occurrences.label: Sulforaphane
occurrences.public_note: One UK broccoli lot, cooked sous vide at 100 °C for 20 minutes, formed 1.06 µmol sulforaphane per g dry weight. Adding 1 g brown mustard powder raised that to 8.58 µmol/g dry weight. Twelve adults who ate 200 g excreted 9.8 µmol sulforaphane-NAC per g creatinine in 24 hours, and 44.7 µmol/g creatinine with the mustard. These figures are not a sulforaphane amount for every 100 g of broccoli.
occurrences.source_note: Okunade et al. (2018), Molecular Nutrition & Food Research 62:1700980, Table 1 and the 24-hour urine result. Table 1, µmol sulforaphane per g dry weight: raw 2.05 ± 0.25; sous vide 100 °C for 20 minutes 1.06 ± 0.18; the same cooked broccoli plus 1 g brown mustard powder 8.58 ± 0.33. 8.58 / 1.06 = 8.1, which the paper reports as an 8-fold increase. One results sentence prints the mustard result as 8.58 ± 0.13; the table figure is used here. Urine, 12 adults, 200 g of that cooked broccoli: 9.8 ± 5.1 µmol sulforaphane-NAC per g creatinine in 24 hours without mustard, and 44.7 ± 33.9 with 1 g mustard. 44.7 / 9.8 = 4.6 from the published means. The paper's average of each person's increase is 4.7-fold, with individual increases from 1.7-fold to 10-fold. Sous-vide myrosinase loss in the same paper: 40% after 2 minutes, 90% after 6 minutes, and no measurable activity after 8 minutes. The study did not report a glucoraphanin concentration, and the dry-weight results are not converted to a fresh 100 g amount. Fahey et al. (1997) identifies sulforaphane as the myrosinase product of glucoraphanin; it is not the source of these figures.

calculation.not_a_panel_amount: Dry-weight and creatinine-normalised study results. No moisture figure is given, so they are not scaled to per 100 g fresh broccoli.

observations.label: 5-Methyltetrahydrofolate
observations.evidence_material: Raw vegetable, analytical sample treated for folate extraction
observations.chemical_form: 5-MTHF equivalents, summed monoglutamate and polyglutamate species
observations.source_reference: Wang, Riedl and Schwartz (2010), Journal of Chromatography B 878(29), 2949–2958, Table 5
observations.source_note: Calculated from the reported Table 5 molar sum, not directly reported mass concentration. Includes polyglutamate species as monoglutamate equivalents, not their intact molecular masses. Glu8 response was estimated by calibration extrapolation; this sample includes that estimated component. Analytical steaming was extraction treatment, not a cooked-food state. One study sample does not establish universal food composition; do not add this vitamer value to total folate as an independent nutrient supply.

limitations: Red-cell DHA is peripheral exposure, not neuronal incorporation, cognition or clinical benefit. No detected DHA group difference; nonsignificance is not equivalence. Post-hoc power could not detect RBC EPA+DHA differences below1.5 percentage points. Small unblinded active-comparator study without untreated control; fish adherence self-reported and groups differed in age. Specified albacore tuna, farmed Atlantic salmon and tested DHA-rich capsules; not arbitrary fish/capsule interchangeability. More fishy aftertaste with capsules; lipid changes do not establish cardiovascular benefit.
selections.delivery: documented composition; PM association does not establish efficacy

limitations: This is a preclinical structural state response, not proof of an indispensable intake or verified new synapse counts. It does not establish human synapse growth, ordinary-food equivalence or cognitive benefit. Developmental mouse marker and visual-response evidence is additional, context-specific support; marker abundance is not an ultrastructurally verified contact count.

limitations: This is supported upstream supply, not a demonstrated dietary constraint on NF-κB. Human precursor supplementation measured red-cell glutathione, not NF-κB; cysteine was supplied as N-acetylcysteine together with glycine.
